definitions.type: real Euclidean vector space with measure
definitions.definition: V=R^n, realized as tuples (x_1,...,x_n). Its topology is the Euclidean topology and its measure dx is the product of n one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. Compactness, continuity and derivatives use these topologies; integrable means Lebesgue absolutely integrable.

W=R^m with inner product v·w=sum_{k=1}^m v_k w_k and norm |v|=(sum_{k=1}^m v_k^2)^(1/2). On V the same convention uses n coordinates. The squared norm and dot product in all formulas have this meaning.

u_t(x,r) is the derivative at r of the one-variable map ρ↦u(x,ρ). Derivatives are ordinary Fréchet derivatives in coordinate directions; outside their differentiability set use the total derivative convention zero. This convention grants no differentiability.

definitions.type: family indexed by j=1,...,n of functions V×(0,∞)→W
definitions.definition: u_j(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u(x,r), the coordinate derivative in the jth spatial direction.

definitions.type: family indexed by j=1,...,n of functions V×(0,∞)→W

definitions.definition: u_jt(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,r). Commutation with ∂_r u_j is a claim to be proved, not part of this definition.
Δu(x,r)=sum_{j=1}^n u_jj(x,r), component by component. The gradient D_x u has columns u_j; its Frobenius square is sum_{j=1}^n |u_j|^2.
e_t(x,r)=∂_r e(x,r), with the total derivative convention of D003.

For each r∈int J the sections of e,e_t,A,B_j,T_j,g_j and ∂_{x_j}g_j (1≤j≤n) are continuous, vanish outside C, have compact support, and are Lebesgue integrable on V. Each is bounded in absolute value on Q and its absolute integral is at most its bound times |Q|. The box Q is compact, measurable, has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞, and C⊂int Q, so all these sections vanish on a neighborhood of ∂Q. In particular e(·,r) is integrable for every r>0.

Let Z be a complete normed additive commutative group and normed real vector space, φ:R→Z and a,b∈R. If φ is differentiable at every z in the unordered closed interval between a and b, and its derivative is interval integrable for Lebesgue measure between a and b, then the oriented interval integral ∫_a^b φ'(z) dz equals φ(b)−φ(a). Interval integrability means integrability on the unordered half-open interval; for a≤b the oriented integral is the Lebesgue integral over (a,b].

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and 1≤j≤n. Choose C,R from N002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n. At t0, g_j, its jth derivative and the two summands B_j,T_j are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C⊂int Q. N003 gives smoothness and the pointwise identity ∂_{x_j}g_j=B_j+T_j.

produces.statement: At t0 the functions g_j, ∂_{x_j}g_j, B_j,T_j are integrable and vanish off C⊂int Q; ∂_{x_j}g_j=B_j+T_j.

argument.text: Define Xhat to be the tuple space of all coordinates except j with product Lebesgue measure, and χ(x)=((x_i)_{i≠j},x_j). Apply M011 with predicate i≠j to split the finite product measure. The remaining block {j} has a unique element; M017 identifies its product measure with ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue measure by evaluation at j. Composing these explicit measurable equivalences shows that χ is a measure-preserving measurable equivalence from V to Xhat×R. The inverse is coordinate insertion. When n=1, Xhat is the one-point empty product with mass one, so the same identification applies.

produces.statement: χ:V→Xhat×R and its inverse are measurable, χ is bijective and preserves dx and the product of the Lebesgue measures on Xhat and R.

argument.text: Fix any y∈Xhat and define G(z)=g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0). By N003 this function is smooth and G'(z)=∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0). If z=±R, the inserted point lies outside C, since C⊂(−R,R)^n; hence G(−R)=G(R)=0. The derivative is continuous on the finite interval [−R,R], so it is interval integrable there. M006 gives ∫_{−R}^R G'(z)dz=G(R)−G(−R)=0. This is also the integral on the closed interval: its endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero. For |z|>R the derivative vanishes by F001; thus ∫_{z∈ℝ} ∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0) dz=0. This proves the zero inner integral for every y, including when some other coordinate lies outside the box.

produces.statement: For every y0∈Xhat, the function z↦∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y0,z),t0) is integrable on the real line and its integral over the real line, equivalently over [−R,R], is zero.

argument.text: Define H(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0). It is continuous by N003 and the explicit coordinate insertion map, and vanishes outside the compact product box corresponding to Q by F001. Thus its support closure is compact. Apply M003 on Xhat×R with its product Lebesgue measure to obtain integrability. Apply M016 with the coordinate equivalence χ and scalar function H: ∫_V ∂_{x_j}g_j(x,t0)dx=∫_{Xhat×R}H. Apply M007 to this integrable H. The product Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite, hence s-finite, including the empty factor. F003 makes each inner integral zero. Therefore ∫_V ∂_{x_j}g_j(x,t0)dx=∫_{Xhat}0=0. Restricting to Q gives the identical box integral, since its integrand vanishes off Q. This is precisely the coordinate FTC/Fubini integration-by-parts step.

Integrate the identity in F001 and use M013 with its two integrable summands B_j(·,t0),T_j(·,t0). F004 yields 0=∫_V B_j+∫_V T_j. Rearranging gives ∫_V B_j=−∫_V T_j. Unfold the definitions of B and T to get exactly the asserted vector-dot-product formula. Generalize over t0>0 and all spatial indices j.
